runs.text: fazerſe dura algũa couſa, q̃ era brãda, & fraca.

lines.note: Continues Tçunori from f0487: something formerly soft and weak becomes hard or strong. The abbreviation q̃ is retained; the scan has a word space before era.
Kano wakai hito wa ikoo tsunotta describes that young man having grown very strong. The opening pilcrow and icǒ, with dotted i, are visible; the Portuguese A- begins Aquelle on the next row.

runs.text: quelle mancebo como creceo, & ſe fez grande

lines.note: Completes Aquelle and begins the explanation that the young man has grown and become big. Grande continues into valente on the next physical row.
Valente completes the description of the strong young man. Isei or ken-i ni tsunoru gives a further example of increasing in power or authority; qen-ini retains its printed internal hyphen.
Ru completes tsunoru. The Portuguese describes growing and rising with honours and pomp; the visible h in honras corrects OCR bonras, while fau- continues below.
Sto completes fauſto, pomp or splendour. Ii tsunoru then means becoming increasingly forceful in speech, as the Portuguese explanation begins to specify.

runs.text: & leuantandoſe no falar como quãdo vai cre-

lines.note: The speaker keeps increasing and raising his manner of speaking. The divided cre- belongs to crecendo below, not to a separate Japanese example.
Completes crecendo: the comparison is to anger growing in someone. This is a short continuation of the preceding speech example.

Tsunoriai, tsunoriau, tsunorioota describes people coming together or meeting. The scan has the internal i omitted by OCR Tçunorai. Acharemſe is the chosen reading for the Portuguese reunion gloss; the nasal letter before ſ is worn and resembles n, so that m remains less secure than the Japanese correction.

runs.text: conhecidas, parentes, ou naturaes da meſma

lines.note: The people are acquaintances, relatives, or natives of the same place. These are parallel descriptions of the persons meeting, continued from the preceding row.

runs.text: terra vendoſe, ou encontrandoſe de nouo, ou

lines.note: The definition specifies people from the same homeland seeing or encountering one another again. Terra completes the expression da mesma terra across the line break.
Depois de muito tempo adds that the reunion may occur after a long interval. This closes the Tçunoriai entry.
Tsunosaki is the tip of a horn, directly matched by ponta do corno. The medial long ſ is retained in the Japanese form.
Tsuppari denotes props or struts. The example tsuppari wo koo begins the Portuguese explanation of placing such supports; the printed caron is retained.

runs.text: põtaletes a algũa parede, ou outra couſa fraca.

lines.note: Completes the prop example: put supports against a wall or another weak object. The abbreviated põtaletes is retained without expanding its nasal mark.

runs.text: Adu. Modo de eſtar algũa couſa

lines.note: Tsuppato is marked as an adverb describing a thing being full. The explanation continues below to the further sense of overflowing.
The gloss adds overflowing, then introduces tsuppato tatayuru as an illustration. Tatayu- is physically divided before ru on the next row.
Ru completes tatayuru; Tresbordar por fora explains overflowing outward. The entire Portuguese word Tresbordar is italic, including its capital T.
Tsuke, tsukuru, tsuketa is the historical verb for putting or attaching one thing to another. Its many following examples distinguish the objects and idioms involved.
Iye ni hi wo tsukuru means setting fire to a house. The Portuguese Por fo- begins the translation across the line break, and Vt is italic apparatus.
Go completes fogo in the house-fire example. Na wo tsukuru introduces assigning or giving a name, glossed Por nome.
Kizu wo tsukuru means inflicting a wound; Ferir supplies the gloss. Iro wo begins the next example about imparting colour.

runs.text: Dar cor, ou tingir, l, per met.

lines.note: Tsukuru completes iro wo tsukuru, to colour or dye. The Portuguese then announces a figurative extension with per met., continued below.
The figurative gloss is to soften matters by giving a better answer. Printed repoſta is retained; Qi begins the alternative ki or kokoro example on the following row.
Ki, alternatively kokoro, wo tsukuru means giving spirit or encouragement. The Portuguese word alento is divided a- / lento across the next boundary.

runs.text: lento ao que eſtà eſmorecido, ou ſem forças.

lines.note: Lento completes alento. The recipient is someone who has become faint, dispirited, or without strength.
The same expression also means applying the mind and attention. Me- introduces me wo tsukuru, directing the eyes, on the next row.

runs.text: Por os olhos em algũa couſa.

lines.note: Wo tsukuru completes me wo tsukuru. The Portuguese explains fixing one’s eyes on something; the Japanese particle remains on its printed physical row.
Kane wo tsukuru refers to colouring the teeth. The Portuguese specifies blackening, with preto carried onto the next line.
Preto completes the tooth-blackening gloss. Koobe wo chi ni tsukuru means placing the head on the ground; Pro- begins the Portuguese verb for prostrating oneself.

runs.text: ſtrarſe com a cabeça por terra. ¶

lines.note: Completes Proſtrarſe: prostration with the head to the earth. The first long ſ and cabeça are supported by the scan, correcting OCR ftrarſe and eabeça; Funeuo starts the next example.

runs.text: Chegar com a embarcação a algũa

lines.note: Fune wo tsukuru means bringing a vessel to a place. The Portuguese begins the explanation with chegar com a embarcação, continued on the following row.

runs.text: parte, ou fazela chegar. ¶ Item, Por;

lines.note: Completes the vessel example as arriving at, or bringing it to, a place. A further sense begins with Item, Por; the semicolon is visibly printed after Por.
The new sense is applying something such as a plaster or medicine. Kizu ni ku- begins kizu ni kusuri wo tsukuru, applying medicine to a wound; como is a single printed word.
Suriuo completes kusuri wo, followed by tsukuru. The Portuguese explicitly gives applying a remedy to the wound, confirming the divided Japanese medicine noun.
Hito ni hito wo tsukuru means assigning someone to accompany another person. The Portuguese starts Mandar algũa and continues directly into the next genuine physical row, c1-l038.

Completes the accompaniment gloss: send a person with another. Ato- starts ato wo tsukuru below. The deleted OCR c1-l037 duplicated fragments from this row and c1-l036; no separate printed line lies between them.
Wo tsukuru completes ato wo tsukuru, here leaving a trail or trace. A further A- begins a repeated form with a pursuit sense on the next line.
The repeated ato wo tsukuru is alternatively ato wo tsukete yuku, to follow a trail. The first form retains its visibly close touotçuquru printing; the Portuguese Ir begins the explanation below.

runs.text: de tras no alcance dos que vão fugindo, ou

lines.note: The following is in pursuit of people who are fleeing. This completes Ir de tras no alcance, with the alternative object continuing onto the next row.
The pursuit may also concern an animal. Teki ga tsukuru then illustrates enemies following in pursuit, with Portuguese I- continued as Irem.

runs.text: rem os inimigos no alcance dos que fogem.

lines.note: Rem completes Irem: enemies go after people who are fleeing. This closes the pursuit example before the summons example below.
Meshibu or origami wo tsukuru introduces sending a written summons or signed order. The opening pilcrow is visible and restored; Mã- begins Mandar across the physical line break.

runs.text: dar patente, ou aſinado a alguem pera o conſ-

lines.note: Completes Mandar patente: send an official document or signed order to someone in order to constrain him. Patente and alguem replace OCR errors; the historical aſinado is retained.
Completes constranger a algũa cousa, compelling someone to an action. Renga wo tsukuru begins a linked-verse example; the visible capital R corrects OCR F.

runs.text: Fazerem dous cada hum ſeu verſo como

lines.note: Ru completes tsukuru. The explanation has two people each composing a verse, like a distich; como is visible rather than OCR conto.
After diſtico closes the renga explanation, tsukeku denotes an attached verse. Tçuqecu and Hũa correct malformed OCR; the definition continues in column 2 with songs or paired verses by two poets.

runs.text: cantigas, ou verſos como diſtico feito por do-

lines.note: Continues the Tçuqecu explanation from column 1: songs or verses like a distich made by two poets. Cantigas and como replace OCR camtigas and cemo; do- continues as dous on the next row.
Us completes dous, followed by poetas: two poets jointly compose the paired verses. This short row belongs to the preceding attached-verse explanation.

A second Tsuke entry introduces the suffixal use after other verbs. The printed principal part quru is retained as supplied, rather than regularized to uru; its q is visible and agrees with the subsequently consulted NINJAL headword record.

runs.text: de outros verbos quer dizer custumarſe, ou ter

lines.note: When joined to another verb’s stem, this verb means becoming accustomed to the action or having a habit of it. Raiz on the preceding row belongs to this grammatical explanation.

runs.text: cuſtume, & habito de fazer algũa couſa. Vt,

lines.note: The explanation completes the sense of having a customary practice or habit of doing something. Habito corrects OCR babito; italic Vt introduces the example on the next line.
Waza wo shitsukuru means being accustomed to work or manual activity. The initial V of Vazauo is visible, correcting OCR Naza; traba- begins trabalhar in the Portuguese gloss.

runs.text: lhar, ou fazer obra de mãos. ¶

lines.note: Lhar completes trabalhar, followed by doing work with the hands. The scan supports obra rather than obta; Fune ni begins the example of a person accustomed to boats.
Nori tsuketa hito describes a person accustomed to riding or travelling aboard a vessel. The Portuguese likewise gives a person accustomed to embarking, continued below; Homem corrects Homam.
Embarking and navigating complete the habitual seafaring example. This short continuation remains a separate physical row.
Tsukeawase means attaching or sticking two things together. The printed ſuru principal part is retained, despite the differing modern paradigm; Pegar is visible rather than OCR Pegas.
Juntando duas cousas completes the divided ajuntando, joining two things. It explains the combining element in the Japanese verb.

Tsukedake is material for kindling a fire, described as a wick, kindling, or a comparable object. Second-pass enlargement shows a dotted i in acendadilhas, correcting OCR acendadalhas; this is the printed Portuguese kindling term.

runs.text: couſa ſemelhante pera acender o fogo.

lines.note: Completes the kindling definition: a similar thing used to light a fire. Couſa, ſemelhante, and acender are supported by the remaining strokes, replacing malformed OCR.
Tsuke ire means driving a fleeing person into a place. The following rows explain the tactical purpose; the printed space between Tçuqe and ire is retained.

runs.text: q̃ vai fugindo em algum lugar pera o prender,

lines.note: The fleeing person is forced into some place so that he can be captured. The abbreviation q̃ and the historical pera are preserved without expansion or modernization.

runs.text: matar, &c. propriamente ſe diz dos inimigos

lines.note: The purpose may also be killing the person. The entry specifies a military use involving enemies; inimigos is supported by the scan, not OCR inimagos.

runs.text: que fazem por força recolher à fortaleza aos q̃

lines.note: The enemies forcibly drive back into a fortress those who had come out. The object aos q̃ continues directly into the next physical row.
Sairão a pelejar identifies those who had sallied out to fight. This completes the description of driving them back into the fortress.

Tsukeire wo suru gives the nominal construction with the same meaning as the preceding verb. The headword’s ei sequence is worn; the repeated Tçuqeireuo and the subsequently consulted NINJAL entry support Tçuqeire over OCR Tçuqoire.
Tsukeito, alternatively neriguri, is prepared silk. The visible capital T corrects OCR I; brã- begins the Portuguese description of the silk as soft.
Da completes branda, soft, with cozida adding boiled or processed. These qualify the beaten silk of the preceding row, rather than forming a new entry.
Tsukemono is something preserved or put in brine. The Portuguese description continues with achar on the following row.
Achar is the Portuguese noun for a pickle or pickled preparation in this list, not an instruction to find something. It closes the tsukemono entry.

Tsukete is glossed acerca, concerning or regarding, and called a participle of the verb Tsuke. Participio corrects OCR Tarticipio; the referenced Japanese Tçuqe is roman within the Portuguese explanation.
Uru completes the cited verb’s principal forms. Kore ni tsukete illustrates concerning this, directly matched by Acerca diſto.

runs.text: Padraſto, ou forte que ſe faz jũ-

lines.note: Tsukeshiro is a siege work or fort constructed near another fortress. Padraſto has its military sense here; jũ- begins junto across the line break.

runs.text: to à fortaleza dos inimigos pera a combater.

lines.note: To completes junto: the work is placed near the enemy fortress in order to attack it. This supplies the purpose of the fort defined above.
Tsukeshiro wo suru means making such a siege fort. The Portuguese Fazer eſte forte refers directly to the construction just described.
Tsuki is identified only as a tree of that name. The worn Portuguese is read Aruore aſi chamada; the gloss does not itself justify supplying a modern botanical species.
Tsuki, tsuku, tsuita means arriving. Minato ni begins the example of reaching a harbour, continued on the next row.
Tsuku completes minato ni tsuku, to arrive at the port. The Portuguese exactly repeats this destination.
Tsuki, illustrated by the honorific otsuki, is an arrival. The Portuguese identifies the arrival of a lord or honoured person; the close printed dalgũſe- is retained.
Nhor completes senhor, followed by a person of honour. This completes the social qualification of the arrival noun.
Tsuki means month or moon. Tsuki ga mitsu- begins the example of the moon becoming full, completed below.
Ru completes mitsuru, becoming full, glossed Serlũa chea. Tsuki ga kakuru introduces the contrary phase, waning; the compact printed Serlũa is retained.
Minguar a lũa explains waning. Tsuki ga kakikumoru then describes the moon becoming obscured or clouded over.
Escurecerſe a lũa completes the obscured-moon example. Tsuki ga teru begins the moon’s shining, with Portuguese A- continued below.

Lumiar completes Alumiar, to illuminate; reſplandecer likewise describes the moon shining. Both the initial l and the n in reſplandecer are visible corrections to OCR; Tçuqiga starts the next example.

runs.text: Estar a lũa clara, & fermoſa. prin-

lines.note: Sayuru completes tsuki ga sayuru, the moon being clear and beautiful. The Portuguese begins a qualification with prin-, completed on the next physical line.

runs.text: cipalmente no Inuerno ſe vſa desta palaura.

lines.note: Cipalmente completes principalmente, explaining that this expression is used especially in winter. The seasonal note belongs to the preceding moon-clarity example.
Tsuki sayete is a poetic expression for the moon being clear, fresh, or cold. P. is the poetry label, kept separate from the italic gloss; lũa corrects OCR ũa.
Fria completes the cold-moon explanation. Tsuki ga tachinoboru introduces the moon rising, and Irſe starts its Portuguese gloss.
Aleuantando a lũa completes the rising-moon explanation. Tsuki no kasa then introduces a halo around the moon; Cir- begins circulo.

runs.text: culo que aparece ao derredor da lũa. ¶

lines.note: Culo completes circulo: the circle appears around the moon. Tçu- begins the next example, tsuki katamuku, on the following physical row.
Qi completes tsuki; katamuku describes the moon inclining or sinking. The Portuguese renders it as descending or lowering, with abaixando- continued below.
Se a lũa completes abaixandoſe a lũa, the moon lowering or setting. The short continuation closes the moon entry before the next verb.

Tsuki, tsuku, tsuita here means striking or thrusting. The Portuguese begins with striking using the hand, chest, and similar means; peitos is visible rather than OCR pritos, and the entry continues on the following page.

The bottom-right italic pera is a catchword anticipating the next page’s continuation. Its final a is abraded and survives chiefly as a right-hand stroke; pera is the chosen reading, not additional body text.
